questions.prompt: What transport does HTTP/3 run over?

options.text: TLS over TCP, same as HTTP/2

questions.explanation: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP — not TCP.

questions.prompt: Why does HTTP/2 still suffer head-of-line blocking?

options.text: All its streams share one TCP connection, and a lost segment stalls everything behind it
It uses text framing that is slow to parse
It opens too many UDP sockets

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes at the application layer but rides one TCP connection; TCP's in-order guarantee means a lost segment blocks all streams (TCP HOL blocking).

questions.prompt: Which advantages does HTTP/3 (QUIC) provide? Select all that apply.

options.text: Independent streams — a lost packet stalls only its own stream
Built-in TLS 1.3 and a faster handshake
Completely different HTTP methods and status codes

questions.explanation: QUIC gives independent streams, built-in TLS 1.3, and connection migration. HTTP semantics (methods/status codes) stay the same across versions.

questions.prompt: HTTP/2 carries many concurrent request/response streams over one TCP connection — a technique called ____.
questions.explanation: Multiplexing interleaves many streams over a single connection, replacing HTTP/1.1's one-request-at-a-time model.

questions.prompt: Match each item to the correct description.

pairs.right: One request/response at a time per connection
Multiplexed binary streams over one TCP connection
HTTP over QUIC (UDP) with independent streams

questions.explanation: 1.1 is serial, 2 multiplexes over TCP, 3 uses QUIC over UDP, and HPACK compresses HTTP/2 headers.

questions.prompt: Order the HTTP versions from oldest to newest.
questions.explanation: The progression is HTTP/1.1, then HTTP/2 (binary/multiplexed over TCP), then HTTP/3 (over QUIC/UDP).
